4 Results
4.1 Net effect
Table 1 shows the five cells. In the cross-system setting
the grounded cell beats the text-only cell on every corpus (F >> T, all
intervals excluding zero).
Self-correction is less clear. A beats C on the synthetic corpus
(+2.92+2.92 pt). On the natural corpora we cannot detect a net difference
(+0.45+0.45 pt, interval [−0.13,+1.05][-0.13,+1.05]; −0.09-0.09 pt, [−1.02,+0.82][-1.02,+0.82]); the
intervals allow about one point either way. On medical speech the interval of
A excludes zero and that of C does not, but the two estimates do not differ.
By net WER alone, the audio does nothing for self-correction on natural
speech. The components tell a different story.
4.2 Repair, damage and break-rate
Table 2 separates the flows. In self-correction the grounded
cell has lower repair and lower damage on all three corpora, and all
six intervals exclude zero. Repair falls by 0.150.15–0.740.74 pt and damage by
0.880.88–2.832.83 pt. With the audio the model simply changes fewer tokens. We
call this restraint, as a description and not as a mechanism.
In the cross-system setting damage also falls on all three corpora, with
intervals excluding zero on two. But repair rises on all three
(+0.09+0.09, +0.95+0.95, +1.25+1.25 pt). On medical dictation it goes from 2.062.06% to
3.313.31% of reference tokens, a 61% relative increase. Part of this rise may
come from the prompts (Section 2.3).
The break-rate shows the restraint directly. In self-correction the text-only
cell breaks 31.9%, 16.3% and 12.8% of the error-free drafts it receives,
although its prompt is the stricter one. The grounded cell breaks 2.6%,
1.0% and 2.3%. In the cross-system setting the text-only cell breaks 18.1%,
4.0% and 13.8%, and the drop is smaller: to 2.6%, 3.0% and 6.9%.
On the natural corpora these rates rest on few error-free inputs, carry no
intervals and include orthographic-only changes, so we read them
descriptively. None of this is visible in aggregate WER there.
Table 3 shows illustrative cases. Without the audio the model
turns the correct draft “loss of hair” into “loss of hearing”; with the
audio it leaves it alone. In the cross-system setting the grounded cell turns
“see you soon” into the correct “seizure”, an edit that the text-only
prompt does not allow. In row 5 the text-only cell swaps one wrong drug name
for another, which the identity does not register.
4.3 Insertions
Why does restraint not lower WER on medical dictation? Because of insertions.
The draft contains insertions worth 4.474.47% of reference tokens. The
text-only cell removes a quarter of them (to 3.293.29%). The grounded cell
leaves the total almost unchanged (4.374.37%). The resulting −1.08-1.08 pt
(interval excluding zero) cancels the +0.98+0.98 pt of the repair and damage
components and gives the net −0.09-0.09 pt.
On RuLibriSpeech the insertion component is small (+0.08+0.08 pt). There the
lost repair offsets much of the reduced damage, and the interval is too wide
to decide.
What are these insertions? Of the 182 inserted tokens in the medical draft,
77 are halves of compounds that the reference writes as one token (“post
operative”, “10 mg”). After the text-only cell 40 such tokens remain. After
the grounded cell 80 remain, and it also adds fillers it hears (“uh”: 6 in
the draft, 14 after grounding).
Each join of a split compound also counts as one repaired token. With no
inverse text normalization, all three components on this corpus are therefore
sensitive to the spelling conventions of the reference, and a compound- and
filler-insensitive scoring could flip the sign of the net A−-C contrast.
Rows 2 and 3 of Table 3 show both sides. The text-only cell
joins “post operative” and corrects a drug name from its own knowledge. The
grounded cell does neither, and the second is a genuine repair that grounding
loses.
4.4 Robustness and the synthetic-corpus ceiling
We recomputed each contrast on the utterances complete for just its own two
cells. No component of Table 2 crosses zero and no interval
changes side. We also scored every missing output as if the corrector had returned its
input unchanged. This sets repair and damage to zero on the imputed rows, so
it is a bound and not a neutral check: the synthetic F−-T repair becomes
+0.31+0.31 instead of +0.09+0.09 pt and damage −0.98-0.98 instead of −1.31-1.31 pt.
Signs and intervals do not depend on the exclusion rule; levels do.
The synthetic corpus sits near its ceiling: 65% of ASR outputs and 79% of
drafts are already exactly correct, so damage is almost the only thing that
can happen. Three of its conclusions do not hold on natural speech.
Text-only self-correction looks very harmful there (−2.78-2.78 pt), while on
the natural corpora its interval includes zero. A second pass without a
hypothesis looks useless or mildly harmful there (+0.01+0.01 pt on the common
subset, −0.38-0.38 pt over all outputs, Table 4) but is the
largest single gain on medical dictation (+2.53+2.53 pt). And the cross-system
repair effect is an order of magnitude smaller there (+0.09+0.09 against +0.95+0.95
and +1.25+1.25 pt).
4.5 Domain terminology, per-domain results and noise
The measurements of Table 4 exist for the synthetic corpus
only and carry the caveat above. Each cell is scored over its own complete
outputs, so columns are not paired and levels differ slightly from
Table 1.
Domain-term recall (DTR) is the share of the corpus’s annotated domain terms
that appear in the output. Text-only self-correction lowers it from 69.069.0%
to 66.166.1%, close to the recogniser (65.565.5%). The grounded cell keeps it
(69.369.3%). In the cross-system setting both cells raise DTR, the grounded one
twice as much (+4.2+4.2 against +2.0+2.0 pt).
T lowers the WER of the ASR output but raises its CER, and C almost quadruples
the CER of the draft. This is consistent with whole words being replaced, not
respelled: without the audio, damage lands on the rare domain words. C raises
the WER of its draft in each of the ten domains (by 1.71.7 to 4.04.0 pt), and A
is better than C in each.
The last rows repeat cells C, A and B on 250 clips, in their original form and
with reverberation (RT60 0.50.5 s) plus pink-and-babble noise at 15 and 8 dB
SNR. The WER of A almost triples. The absolute gap between C and A stays at
2.842.84, 2.962.96 and 2.892.89 pt, while the relative gap narrows (C/A from 2.32.3
to 1.51.5). We did not decompose the noisy runs, so this shows that the WER gap
persists, not that the restraint does. The cost of withholding the hypothesis
(B against A) grows from 0.570.57 to 1.431.43 pt.

4.6 Other models
Table 5 repeats all cells with Voxtral-Small-24B on a
659-utterance subset of the same clips. Its text-only self-correction rarely
edits: the fix-rate of cell C is 1.5–3.8%, against 24.2–27.8% for Gemini
(not tabulated).
Here the pattern of Gemini does not replicate. The grounded cell has
higher repair in all six contrasts (+0.24+0.24 to +4.64+4.64 pt), four with
intervals excluding zero, and repair rises even against Voxtral’s own draft.
Damage moves inconsistently: it falls on medical dictation in both settings
and rises elsewhere. The insertion component, obtained by subtraction, is the
largest of the three in self-correction and makes the net A−-C contrast
negative on two of three corpora.
In our two models, then, restraint is not a property of the acoustic channel
as such. It is consistent with what grounding does to a corrector that would
otherwise over-correct.
GPT Audio calls for the same caution. In cell F it degrades two of three
corpora (by 8.828.82 and 8.548.54 pt) with break-rates of 21.3% and 31.4%. These
figures carry no intervals and cover only clips with a usable output.
Cell B suggests a second role of the hypothesis. On medical dictation Voxtral
without a hypothesis goes from a WER of 43.8643.86% to 65.0165.01%, and 99.699.6% of
that degradation is the insertion component: it emits 0.500.50 inserted words
per reference token. Here the hypothesis bounded the output length, but the interval
includes zero and the opposite holds on RuLibriSpeech (+6.09+6.09 pt).
